notes.front: What does Scrum.org call the essence of self-management?
notes.back: The room and empowerment a team is given to decide how to do its own work, instead of being directed.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org ties this to complex work, where there is no known recipe and the team must find its way by experimenting.
notes.example: Like a restaurant owner who tells the kitchen which dishes the menu needs but lets the chefs decide who cooks what and how.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Self-Managing Teams”, “Why does Scrum require Self-Managing Teams?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Scrum Teams are self-managing, meaning they internally decide {{c1::who does what, when, and how}}.
notes.back: who does what, when, and how
notes.explanation: The Guide pairs this with being cross-functional: the members have all the skills needed to create value each Sprint.
notes.evidence: Scrum Teams are cross-functional, meaning the members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint. They are also self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how.

notes.front: Each morning the Product Owner tells each Developer which task to pick up and how long it should take. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: That is for the team: a self-managing Scrum Team internally decides who does what, when and how.
notes.choices:
A) Fine: the Product Owner is accountable for the work, so assigns it
B) That is for the team: a self-managing Scrum Team internally decides who does what, when and how
C) Fine, as long as the Scrum Master agrees
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Product Owner's accountability does not include deciding who does what; the Guide leaves that to the team. C: the Scrum Master's approval does not change who decides.
notes.explanation: Self-management, as the Guide defines it, puts the who, when and how inside the team.
notes.evidence: They are also self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how.

notes.front: Why does Scrum.org say teams facing complex problems rarely succeed by following one person's detailed instructions?
notes.back: There is no known recipe for such problems; the team has to experiment its way to a solution.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org describes the team forming hypotheses, testing them and acting on what it learns.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Self-Managing Teams”, “Why does Scrum require Self-Managing Teams?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to Scrum.org, what is the best way to support a team working on a complex problem?
notes.back: Give it room to decide how to do its work, instead of directing it.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org calls this room, together with empowerment, the core of self-management.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Self-Managing Teams”, “Why does Scrum require Self-Managing Teams?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team is building a fraud-detection feature nobody in the company has built before. A department head sends a 30-step plan of exactly how to build it. What fits Scrum.org's view of self-managing teams?
notes.back: Let the team work out how, by experimenting, rather than directing it step by step.
notes.choices:
A) Follow the plan exactly, since it removes uncertainty
B) Let the team work out how, by experimenting, rather than directing it step by step
C) Ask the Product Owner to turn the plan into daily task assignments
notes.choicesExplained: A: for a new, complex problem Scrum.org says following someone's instructions rarely succeeds. C: daily assignments are still directing the team rather than giving it room.
notes.explanation: For work where there is no known recipe, Scrum.org says the team finds the answer through experiments.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Self-Managing Teams”, “Why does Scrum require Self-Managing Teams?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of the Developers' accountabilities concerns creating the Sprint Backlog?
notes.back: Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists making this plan among what the Developers are always accountable for, whatever skills the work needs.
notes.evidence: Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog;

notes.front: Through what are the Developers accountable for instilling quality?
notes.back: By adhering to a Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: Quality is built in by meeting the Definition of Done, which is one of the Developers' standing accountabilities.
notes.evidence: Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done;

notes.front: How often, and toward what, are the Developers accountable for adapting their plan?
notes.back: Each day, toward the Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: The plan is not fixed at Sprint Planning; the Developers adjust it daily with the Sprint Goal as the target.
notes.evidence: Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal; and,

notes.front: Which of the Developers' accountabilities is about how they treat one another?
notes.back: Holding each other accountable as professionals.
notes.explanation: It is the last of the four things the Guide says Developers are always accountable for.
notes.evidence: Holding each other accountable as professionals.

notes.front: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for {{c1::the Developers}}.
notes.back: the Developers
notes.explanation: The Guide calls it a highly visible, real-time picture of the work the Developers plan for the Sprint Goal, updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.evidence: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal. Consequently, the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.

notes.front: Mid-Sprint, a Product Owner quietly rewrites the Developers' task breakdown in the Sprint Backlog to reflect how she would build it. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers; they own and update it.
notes.choices:
A) Fine: the Product Owner orders all backlogs
B) The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers; they own and update it
C) Fine, as long as the Sprint Goal does not change
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog; the Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers. C: keeping the Sprint Goal does not make the Developers' plan hers to rewrite.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the Sprint Backlog the Developers' own plan, which they update as they learn.
notes.evidence: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers.

notes.front: Whose commitment is the Sprint Goal, and what does it leave flexible?
notes.back: It is a commitment by the Developers; it leaves flexible the exact work needed to achieve it.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the goal also creates coherence and focus, encouraging the Scrum Team to work together rather than on separate initiatives.
notes.evidence: Although the Sprint Goal is a commitment by the Developers, it provides flexibility in terms of the exact work needed to achieve it. The Sprint Goal also creates coherence and focus, encouraging the Scrum Team to work together rather than on separate initiatives.

notes.front: If the work turns out different than expected, the Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without {{c1::affecting the Sprint Goal}}.
notes.back: affecting the Sprint Goal
notes.explanation: The goal stays fixed while the scope of work toward it can move.
notes.evidence: If the work turns out to be different than they expected, they collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.

notes.front: Halfway through a Sprint whose goal is “customers can reset their password by text message”, the Developers find one planned item, a new email template, is much bigger than expected and not needed for the goal. What should they do?
notes.back: Negotiate the Sprint Backlog's scope with the Product Owner, keeping the Sprint Goal intact.
notes.choices:
A) Negotiate the Sprint Backlog's scope with the Product Owner, keeping the Sprint Goal intact
B) Change the Sprint Goal to match whatever they can finish
C) Work overtime and lower testing to finish everything as planned
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide has scope negotiated without affecting the Sprint Goal. C: the Guide says quality does not decrease during the Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Guide's route when work differs from expectations is scope negotiation with the Product Owner, not a new goal.
notes.evidence: If the work turns out to be different than they expected, they collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.

notes.front: During the Sprint, what kind of change does the Scrum Guide say is not made?
notes.back: Any change that would endanger the Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: Other change is possible; the Sprint Goal is what is protected.
notes.evidence: No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal;

notes.front: During the Sprint, quality {{c1::does not decrease}}.
notes.back: does not decrease
notes.explanation: The same list protects the Sprint Goal from changes that would endanger it.
notes.evidence: Quality does not decrease;

notes.front: During the Sprint, what happens to the Product Backlog?
notes.back: It is refined as needed.
notes.explanation: It is one of the four conditions the Guide lists for the time during a Sprint.
notes.evidence: The Product Backlog is refined as needed; and,

notes.front: During the Sprint, what may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned?
notes.back: Scope.
notes.explanation: Scope can move with learning; the Sprint Goal and quality do not.
notes.evidence: Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.

notes.front: Two days before the Sprint ends, a stakeholder urges the Developers to skip code review so that every Sprint Backlog item gets finished. Which rule of the Sprint does this break?
notes.back: Quality does not decrease during the Sprint.
notes.choices:
A) Quality does not decrease during the Sprint
B) The Product Backlog is refined as needed
C) None: the Developers decide how to work, so anything goes
notes.choicesExplained: B: refinement is unrelated to cutting review. C: self-management covers how the work is done, but the Guide still says quality does not decrease.
notes.explanation: Cutting review to hit volume trades away quality, which the Guide rules out during the Sprint.
notes.evidence: Quality does not decrease;

notes.front: The Scrum Team is small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically {{c1::10 or fewer}} people.
notes.back: 10 or fewer
notes.explanation: The Guide says that, in general, smaller teams communicate better and are more productive.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team is small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically 10 or fewer people. In general, we have found that smaller teams communicate better and are more productive.

notes.front: A Scrum Team has grown to 16 people working on one product, and communication is struggling. What does the Scrum Guide suggest?
notes.back: Consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams on the same product, sharing one Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) Split into two teams, each with its own Product Owner and Product Backlog
B) Consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams on the same product, sharing one Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner
C) Keep one team but appoint a team lead for each half
notes.choicesExplained: A: teams on the same product should share the Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner. C: the Guide says there are no sub-teams or hierarchies within a Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: The Guide's advice for teams grown too large keeps one product direction across the new teams.
notes.evidence: If Scrum Teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product. Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

notes.front: What does the Scrum Guide say about sub-teams and hierarchies within a Scrum Team?
notes.back: There are none.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes the team as a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal.
notes.evidence: Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies. It is a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal.

notes.front: A manager proposes that, inside one Scrum Team, three Developers form a “testing sub-team” reporting to a senior tester. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: Within a Scrum Team there are no sub-teams or hierarchies.
notes.choices:
A) Fine, if it speeds up testing
B) Within a Scrum Team there are no sub-teams or hierarchies
C) Fine, as long as the senior tester is also the Scrum Master
notes.choicesExplained: A: speed does not create an exception to the rule. C: adding a hierarchy is the problem, whoever sits at the top.
notes.explanation: The Guide keeps the Scrum Team a single cohesive unit focused on the Product Goal.
notes.evidence: Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies.

notes.front: Who does the Scrum Guide hold accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint?
notes.back: The entire Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: Within that shared accountability the Guide then defines three specific ones: Developers, Product Owner and Scrum Master.
notes.evidence: The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint. Scrum defines three specific accountabilities within the Scrum Team: the Developers, the Product Owner, and the Scrum Master.

notes.front: A Sprint ends with no useful Increment. At the Sprint Retrospective the Product Owner says “that's the Developers' problem; I only order the backlog.” How does this square with the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: It does not: the entire Scrum Team, Product Owner included, is accountable for a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.
notes.choices:
A) Correct: only the Developers are accountable for the Increment
B) It does not: the entire Scrum Team, Product Owner included, is accountable for a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint
C) Correct: the Scrum Master is accountable for the Increment
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Developers create the Increment, but the Guide makes the entire Scrum Team accountable for it. C: the Guide places this accountability on the entire Scrum Team, not the Scrum Master alone.
notes.explanation: The Guide assigns this accountability to the whole team before it names the three specific accountabilities.
notes.evidence: The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.

notes.front: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of {{c1::eight hours}} for a one-month Sprint.
notes.back: eight hours
notes.explanation: For shorter Sprints the Guide says the event is usually shorter.
notes.evidence: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

notes.front: If an organization implements only parts of Scrum, is the result Scrum?
notes.back: No. The framework is immutable; implementing only parts is possible, but the result is not Scrum.
notes.explanation: The Guide says Scrum exists only in its entirety, and works well as a container for other techniques and practices.
notes.evidence: The Scrum framework, as outlined herein, is immutable. While implementing only parts of Scrum is possible, the result is not Scrum. Scrum exists only in its entirety and functions well as a container for other techniques, methodologies, and practices.

notes.front: During a Sprint, how does the Sprint Goal differ from the scope of the Sprint Backlog in what may change?
notes.back: The Sprint Goal is protected; the Sprint Backlog's scope may be negotiated with the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide lets scope be renegotiated as more is learned, but only without affecting the Sprint Goal.
notes.evidence: they collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.

notes.front: On day 2 the Developers learn that a planned database change is unnecessary, but they leave the Sprint Backlog untouched until the Sprint ends. Which accountability of theirs are they neglecting?
notes.back: Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal.
notes.choices:
A) Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal
B) Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done
C) Ordering the Product Backlog
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing here lowers quality or skips the Definition of Done. C: ordering the Product Backlog is not one of the Developers' accountabilities.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes adapting the plan toward the Sprint Goal a daily accountability, not an end-of-Sprint one.
notes.evidence: Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal; and,
